From Intent to Evidence: A Categorical Approach for Structural Evaluation of Deep Research Agents

Shuoling Liu    Zhiquan Tan    Kun Yi    Hui Wu    Yihan Li    Jiangpeng Yan    Liyuan Chen    Kai Chen    Qiang Yang1. The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology2. E Fund Management Co., Ltd.3. The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
Abstract

Although deep research agents (DRAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for complex information synthesis, their evaluation remains constrained by ad hoc empirical benchmarks. These heuristic approaches do not rigorously model agent behavior or adequately stress-test long-horizon synthesis and ambiguity resolution. To bridge this gap, we formalize DRA behavior through the lens of category theory, modeling deep research workflow as a composition of structure-preserving maps (functors). Grounded in this theoretical framework, we introduce a novel mechanism-aware benchmark with 296 questions designed to stress-test agents along four interpretable axes: traversing sequential connectivity chains, verifying intersections within V-structure pullbacks, imposing topological ordering on retrieved substructures, and performing ontological falsification via the Yoneda Probe. Our rigorous evaluation of 11 leading models establishes a persistently low baseline, with the state-of-the-art achieving only a 19.9% average accuracy, exposing the difficulty of formal structural stress-testing. Furthermore, our findings reveal a stark dichotomy in the current AI capabilities. While advanced deep research pipelines successfully redefine dynamic topological re-ordering and exhibit robust ontological verification---matching pure reasoning models in falsifying hallucinated premises---they almost universally collapse on multi-hop structural synthesis. Crucially, massive performance variance across tasks exposes a lingering reliance on brittle heuristics rather than a systemic understanding. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that while top-tier autonomous agents can now organically unify search and reasoning, achieving a generalized mastery over complex structural information remains a formidable open challenge.11 1 Our implementation will be available at https://github.com/tzq1999/CDR.

1 Introduction

The recent leap in large language models (LLMs) has sparked the rapid development of autonomous agents, with Deep Research Agents (DRAs) emerging as a practical solution for complex tasks (Wu et al., 2025). Unlike early systems confined to static knowledge recall (Wei et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025), true deep research is inherently dynamic (Nie et al., 2024). It requires an agent to actively seek out, cross-validate, and stitch together information from diverse and frequently conflicting sources (Hu et al., 2025). To provide genuine decision support, a DRA must go beyond simple retrieval; it needs to master the art of filtering noise, resolving contradictions, and synthesizing fragmented evidence into well-grounded judgments (Du et al., 2025).

However, a rigorous theoretical modeling of deep research agent behavior remains conspicuously absent from the literature. Without a formal mathematical foundation, current evaluation paradigms rely heavily on purely empirical and ad-hoc designs (Xu and Peng, 2025). These heuristic benchmarks lack the systematism required to explicitly disentangle and measure an agent’s concrete capabilities, often blurring the lines between genuine reasoning, basic retrieval, and simple memorization (Shi et al., 2025). Compounding this issue is the limited complexity of the evaluation tasks themselves; the queries designed in existing datasets rarely pose the level of difficulty needed to genuinely stress-test an agent’s capacity for long-horizon synthesis and ambiguity resolution. This highlights a critical gap: the community lacks a theoretically grounded benchmark that provides both systematic capability verification and appropriately challenging tasks. Addressing this requires a fundamental shift from fragmented empirical testing toward a formal framework capable of rigorously modeling, and subsequently evaluating, the agent’s entire research ability.

We formalize the behavior of the Deep Research Agent through the lens of category theory (Mac Lane, 2013), since the deep-research workflow is fundamentally a structural mapping: an abstract intent is mediated through a noisy external web and transformed into a logically constrained conclusion space. Rather than treating the pipeline as an ad-hoc collection of heuristics, this perspective models the workflow as a composition of structure-preserving maps (functors), which enables precise, testable statements about agent behaviours. Grounded in this categorical framework, we systematically construct a challenging benchmark with 296 bilingual questions that adversarially stress-tests agents along four interpretable axes: traversing sequential connectivity chains, verifying intersections within V-structure pullbacks, imposing topological ordering on retrieved substructures, and performing ontological falsification via the Yoneda Probe—so as to provide diagnostic, mechanism-aware evaluations. See Figure 1 for an illustrative view.

We systematically benchmark 1111 leading models across reasoning, search-augmented, and autonomous deep research paradigms using a strict, human-verified evaluation pipeline. The results establish a persistently low baseline—with the state-of-the-art achieving only a 19.9%19.9\% average—rigorously exposing the profound difficulty of formal structural stress-testing. Our evaluation reveals a stark dichotomy in current AI capabilities. On one hand, advanced deep research pipelines demonstrate emerging strengths: they successfully redefine dynamic topological re-ordering and exhibit robust ontological verification, matching pure reasoning models in their ability to falsify hallucinated premises. On the other hand, critical vulnerabilities remain unresolved. Models almost universally collapse on multi-hop structural synthesis and exhibit absolute blind spots under specific mathematical constraints. Crucially, the massive performance variance both within the deep research paradigm and across individual tasks indicates a lingering reliance on brittle heuristics rather than a systemic understanding. Ultimately, these findings underscore that while top-tier autonomous agents can now organically unify search and reasoning, achieving a generalized mastery over complex structural topologies remains a formidable open challenge.

2 Preliminary

To formalize the behavior of deep research agents, we briefly introduce several foundational concepts from category theory (Mac Lane, 2013). Our presentation balances mathematical precision with intuitive interpretations tailored for machine learning.

Definition 2.1 (Category).

A category 𝒞\mathcal{C} consists of a class of objects Ob⁡(𝒞)\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{C}) and, for any pair of objects X,Y∈Ob⁡(𝒞)X,Y\in\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{C}), a set of morphisms Hom𝒞​(X,Y)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y). These morphisms are equipped with a composition law: for f∈Hom𝒞​(X,Y)f\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y) and g∈Hom𝒞​(Y,Z)g\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y,Z), their composition g∘f∈Hom𝒞​(X,Z)g\circ f\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Z) is associative. Furthermore, every object XX has an identity morphism idX∈Hom𝒞​(X,X)\mathrm{id}_{X}\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,X).

Intuition in ML: A category abstracts a system of objects and their structure-preserving transformations. In our context, objects naturally correspond to representation spaces, datasets, or hypothesis classes, while morphisms represent the functions, network layers, or reasoning paths that map between them.

Definition 2.2 (Functor).

Given categories 𝒞\mathcal{C} and 𝒟\mathcal{D}, a functor F:𝒞→𝒟F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D} is a structure-preserving mapping that assigns each object X∈𝒞X\in\mathcal{C} to an object F⁡(X)∈𝒟F(X)\in\mathcal{D}, and each morphism f:X→Yf:X\to Y in 𝒞\mathcal{C} to a morphism F⁡(f):F⁡(X)→F⁡(Y)F(f):F(X)\to F(Y) in 𝒟\mathcal{D}. A functor must preserve composition, i.e., F⁡(g∘f)=F⁡(g)∘F⁡(f)F(g\circ f)=F(g)\circ F(f), and identity, i.e., F⁡(idX)=idF⁡(X)F(\mathrm{id}_{X})=\mathrm{id}_{F(X)}.

Intuition in ML: Functors provide a principled way to translate between different architectural paradigms or representation spaces. They ensure that the relational structure (the morphisms) of the original space is perfectly preserved during the mapping—analogous to how parameterization or embedding functions map discrete symbolic spaces into continuous latent spaces while preserving semantic relationships.

Definition 2.3 (Pullback).

Given an object ZZ and two morphisms f:X→Zf:X\to Z and g:Y→Zg:Y\to Z, their pullback is an object PP equipped with projection morphisms π1:P→X\pi_{1}:P\to X and π2:P→Y\pi_{2}:P\to Y such that f∘π1=g∘π2f\circ\pi_{1}=g\circ\pi_{2}. Furthermore, PP satisfies a universal property: for any object QQ with morphisms u:Q→Xu:Q\to X and v:Q→Yv:Q\to Y satisfying f∘u=g∘vf\circ u=g\circ v, there exists a unique morphism h:Q→Ph:Q\to P such that π1∘h=u\pi_{1}\circ h=u and π2∘h=v\pi_{2}\circ h=v.

Intuition in ML: The pullback computes the most general object whose images in XX and YY are consistent under ff and gg. In the category of sets, it is given by P={(x,y)∈X×Y∣f⁡(x)=g⁡(y)}P=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y\mid f(x)=g(y)\}. In machine learning, computing a pullback corresponds to enforcing equality constraints or performing multimodal fusion, where representations from different modalities (XX and YY) must align in a shared abstract semantic space (ZZ).

Definition 2.4 (Limits and Colimits).

Let JJ be an index category and D:J→𝒞D:J\to\mathcal{C} be a diagram (a functor) in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The limit of DD, denoted limD\lim D, is an object L∈𝒞L\in\mathcal{C} equipped with projection morphisms πj:L→D⁡(j)\pi_{j}:L\to D(j) that are compatible with all morphisms in DD, satisfying a universal property analogous to the pullback. Dually, the colimit of DD, denoted colim⁡D\operatorname{colim}D, is the limit of the corresponding diagram in the opposite category 𝒞op\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}} (where all morphism directions are reversed).

Intuition in ML: Limits and colimits generalize the notions of aggregation and composition. A limit (which encompasses products and pullbacks) aggregates information by finding the maximal jointly consistent representation that satisfies multiple structural constraints across the diagram. Conversely, a colimit (which encompasses disjoint unions and pushouts) formalizes the process of "gluing" or ensembling objects together—such as merging distinct state spaces or representations along a shared subspace.

3 Categorical Formulation of Deep Research Agents

We formalize the end-to-end workflow of a Deep Research Agent (DRA) as a structural mapping from an abstract problem space to a structured conclusion space, fundamentally mediated by an external knowledge environment (the Web). While the empirical behaviors of large language models (LLMs) are often described using heuristic terminology, casting this transition into the language of category theory allows us to strictly define the requisite capabilities of an ideal DRA—such as task decomposition, information retrieval, and logical synthesis—through standard categorical constructs. More importantly, it provides a rigorous mathematical vocabulary to diagnose common agentic failure modes. More detailed proofs can be found in Appendix A. An illustrative figure can be found in Figure 2.

3.1 Agent State Spaces as Categories

Before defining the functors that govern the agent’s dynamic behavior, we first establish the foundational categories that represent the distinct state spaces of the research process. For each conceptual phase, we specify its objects (Ob\mathrm{Ob}) and morphisms (Hom\mathrm{Hom}) to seamlessly bridge formal mathematics with intuitive AI operations.

The Intent Category 𝒬\mathcal{Q} (Query Space). The starting point of any research task resides in the Intent Space, which encapsulates the informational goals of the agent. Here, the objects q∈Ob⁡(𝒬)q\in\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{Q}) represent all possible user queries, sub-problems, or atomic intent units. The morphisms Hom𝒬​(q1,q2)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{Q}}(q_{1},q_{2}) represent task dependency or refinement. Specifically, a directed morphism q1→depq2q_{1}\xrightarrow{\text{dep}}q_{2} exists if resolving the sub-problem q2q_{2} strictly depends on the resolution of q1q_{1}. In the context of autonomous agents, this category effectively models and formalizes the agent’s internal task decomposition and planning graph.

The Knowledge Category 𝒲\mathcal{W} (Web Space). To execute these intents, the agent operates within the Knowledge Space, representing the vast, interconnected external environment. Its objects w∈Ob⁡(𝒲)w\in\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{W}) are informational entities on the World Wide Web, such as web pages, raw documents, code snippets, or database records. The morphisms Hom𝒲​(w1,w2)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{W}}(w_{1},w_{2}) denote structural or evidentiary linkages. A morphism w1→refw2w_{1}\xrightarrow{\text{ref}}w_{2} exists if w1w_{1} contains a hyperlink to w2w_{2}, or if the semantic content of w1w_{1} objectively acts as a supporting premise or causal relation for w2w_{2}.

The Retrieval Subcategory 𝐒𝐮𝐛⁡(𝒲)\mathbf{Sub}(\mathcal{W}) (Retrieved Context). Because LLMs operate with finite context windows, the agent cannot process the entire Web simultaneously; instead, it interacts with a localized Retrieval Subspace. This is defined as a category formed by subgraphs (subcategories) of 𝒲\mathcal{W}. Its objects G∈Ob⁡(𝐒𝐮𝐛⁡(𝒲))G\in\mathrm{Ob}(\mathbf{Sub}(\mathcal{W})) are the retrieved knowledge subgraphs G⊆𝒲G\subseteq\mathcal{W} collected by the agent at any given step. The morphisms Hom𝐒𝐮𝐛​(G1,G2)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Sub}}(G_{1},G_{2}) are inclusion mappings (G1↪G2G_{1}\hookrightarrow G_{2}) or morphism restrictions. Intuitively, these mappings formalize the monotonic accumulation of gathered evidence as the agent systematically explores the Web.

The Reasoning Category 𝒜\mathcal{A} (Logic/Answer Space). Finally, the synthesized outputs reside in the Reasoning Category, which captures the internal cognitive workspace where final reports are synthesized. The objects a∈Ob⁡(𝒜)a\in\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{A}) are formulated propositions, intermediate arguments, or final factual statements. The morphisms Hom𝒜​(a1,a2)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(a_{1},a_{2}) represent strict logical entailment. A morphism a1→impliesa2a_{1}\xrightarrow{\text{implies}}a_{2} exists if proposition a1a_{1} is a sufficient condition, or provides robust deductive backing, for proposition a2a_{2} (a1⟹a2a_{1}\implies a_{2}).

Theorem 3.1 (Categorical Validity of Agentic State Spaces).

Let 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, 𝒲\mathcal{W}, 𝐒𝐮𝐛⁡(𝒲)\mathbf{Sub}(\mathcal{W}), and 𝒜\mathcal{A} be the agentic state spaces equipped with their respective objects and relations. If we define the morphisms in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, 𝒲\mathcal{W}, and 𝒜\mathcal{A} as above, then all four spaces strictly satisfy the Eilenberg-Mac Lane axioms and thus constitute mathematically valid categories.

Equipped with these formal state spaces, the overarching deep research process can now be elegantly modeled as a sequence of structure-preserving functors bridging 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, 𝐒𝐮𝐛⁡(𝒲)\mathbf{Sub}(\mathcal{W}), and 𝒜\mathcal{A}, which will concretely define the agent’s core capabilities of searching and reasoning.

3.2 Agent Workflows as Functors

Search Functor

We formalize the (ideal) search operation as a functor S:𝒬→𝐒𝐮𝐛⁡(𝒲)S:\mathcal{Q}\to\mathbf{Sub}(\mathcal{W}) that maps an abstract “problem flow” to a concrete “evidence flow.” An ideal search functor must satisfy two central categorical conditions—preservation of morphisms and preservation of composition—while the remaining conditions (object mapping and identity preservation) are typically straightforward to satisfy.

Definition 3.2 (Morphism Mapping and Dependency Preservation).

For any query dependency f:q1→q2f:q_{1}\to q_{2} in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, the Search Functor must map it to a valid morphism S⁡(f):S⁡(q1)→S⁡(q2)S(f):S(q_{1})\to S(q_{2}) within the retrieval subspace.

Remark 3.3 (Semantic interpretation of search dependency).

Definition 3.2 constrains the agent’s search trajectory. If a question q2q_{2} logically depends on q1q_{1}, then the retrieved material subobject S⁡(q2)∈𝐒𝐮𝐛⁡(𝒲)S(q_{2})\in\mathbf{Sub}(\mathcal{W}) should extend S⁡(q1)S(q_{1}) in the categorical sense: there exists a monomorphism ι:S⁡(q1)↪S⁡(q2)\iota:S(q_{1})\hookrightarrow S(q_{2}) in 𝐒𝐮𝐛⁡(𝒲)\mathbf{Sub}(\mathcal{W}). (When 𝐒𝐮𝐛⁡(𝒲)\mathbf{Sub}(\mathcal{W}) is realised as a poset of concrete subsets, this condition reduces to S⁡(q1)⊆S⁡(q2)S(q_{1})\subseteq S(q_{2}).)

In practice, this means S⁡(q2)S(q_{2}) ought to organically extend S⁡(q1)S(q_{1})—for example, by including pages reachable via hyperlinks appearing in S⁡(q1)S(q_{1}), or by containing temporal successors in a time-series search. Accordingly, when an agent decomposes a problem into subquestions, it should preserve and make available the entire set of previously accessed material (i.e., the access history/provenance) associated with those subquestions.

Proposition 3.4 (Chain-of-Search Consistency).

An ideal deep research agent preserves compositionality during multi-hop retrieval (deep search). For a sequence of sub-task dependencies q1→𝑓q2→𝑔q3q_{1}\xrightarrow{f}q_{2}\xrightarrow{g}q_{3}, it strictly holds that S⁡(g∘f)=S⁡(g)∘S⁡(f)S(g\circ f)=S(g)\circ S(f).

The Reasoning Functor

The logical synthesis process is formally defined as an ideal functor R:𝒲→𝒜R:\mathcal{W}\to\mathcal{A}. It represents the fundamental capability of the agent to map unstructured entities from the global web knowledge space 𝒲\mathcal{W} into structured propositions in the abstract logic space 𝒜\mathcal{A}. (In practice, during a specific task, this functor acts upon the retrieved evidence subgraph Im⁡(S)\mathrm{Im}(S)).

Definition 3.5 (Morphism Mapping and Causality Preservation).

For any evidentiary morphism f∈Hom𝒲​(w1,w2)f\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{W}}(w_{1},w_{2})—such as a hyperlink or an objective causal premise—the reasoning functor must produce a valid logical implication R⁡(f)∈Hom𝒜​(R⁡(w1),R⁡(w2))R(f)\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(R(w_{1}),R(w_{2})). Consequently, for any such pair (w1,w2)(w_{1},w_{2}), the functor induces a mapping between hom-sets: Rw1,w2:Hom𝒲​(w1,w2)→Hom𝒜​(R⁡(w1),R⁡(w2))R_{w_{1},w_{2}}:\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{W}}(w_{1},w_{2})\to\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(R(w_{1}),R(w_{2})). This ensures that the generated logic is strictly anchored to objective external evidence.

Remark 3.6 (Formal Characterization of Hallucination).

In categorical terms, an agent hallucinates precisely when the induced mapping Rw1,w2R_{w_{1},w_{2}} is not surjective (not full functor). If the agent asserts a target morphism h∈Hom𝒜​(R⁡(w1),R⁡(w2))h\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(R(w_{1}),R(w_{2})) such that h∉Im⁡(Rw1,w2)h\notin\mathrm{Im}(R_{w_{1},w_{2}}), this assertion is explicitly hallucinatory. The agent has fabricated a logical implication hh that lacks any valid evidentiary pre-image. The most extreme manifestation occurs when Hom𝒲​(w1,w2)=∅\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{W}}(w_{1},w_{2})=\varnothing (no evidentiary link exists whatsoever), yet the agent still asserts hh, effectively generating deductive claims out of thin air.

Proposition 3.7 (Functoriality and Transitivity of Deduction).

By the composition axiom of functors, an ideal reasoning agent inherently preserves deductive transitivity. For any composable evidentiary morphisms w1→𝑓w2→𝑔w3w_{1}\xrightarrow{f}w_{2}\xrightarrow{g}w_{3} in 𝒲\mathcal{W}, it strictly holds that R⁡(g∘f)=R⁡(g)∘R⁡(f)R(g\circ f)=R(g)\circ R(f).

Report Generation

The ultimate objective of a deep research process is to synthesize a final report for a given query qq. The Reasoning Functor RR transforms all retrieved fragmented evidence from S⁡(q)S(q) into a structural graph of partial arguments within 𝒜\mathcal{A}. From the defintion from standard textbook (Mac Lane, 2013), we should formulate the final report, denoted as R​e​p​(q)Rep(q), as the colimit of this graph: R​e​p​(q)≅colim​R​(S⁡(q))Rep(q)\cong\text{colim}R(S(q)).

Consequently, if the report generated by an agent fails to become a colimit—for instance, if conflicting conclusions remain unresolved, or if fabricated summaries are added—it indicates that the deep research process is non-natural during the aggregation stage.

4 Design of Evaluation

The inherent scale and topological complexity of the real-world knowledge and logic categories pose significant challenges to the strict functoriality of an agent’s Search and Reasoning operations. To systematically quantify an agent’s capacity for structural preservation against phenomena like context truncation and hallucination, we propose a four-dimensional categorical evaluation framework:

  • •

    Connectivity via Simple Chains: Evaluating the agent’s ability to perform linear, transitive reasoning across sequential information nodes.

  • •

    Consistency via V-Structures (Pullbacks): Assessing the agent’s capacity to handle multi-source verification, intersection finding, and conflict resolution.

  • •

    Organization via Substructure Re-ordering: Testing the agent’s skill in disentangling complex dependencies and restructuring chaotic information into ordered flows.

  • •

    Structure Validity via the Yoneda Probe: Verifying the ontological reality of entities by probing their external relationships and behavioral definitions, rather than relying solely on internal attributes.

4.1 Type I: Connectivity via Simple Chains

We ground the design of Type I tasks in the principle of Retrieval-Verification Asymmetry. Specifically, we construct queries where the forward search path (Problem →\to Answer) requires traversing an obscure, step-by-step trajectory, while the backward verification path (Answer →\to Problem) remains computationally straightforward. In this type, each node entity can be found on a single webpage link.

To simulate the practical complexities of deep research, we decompose linear reasoning into three distinct sub-tasks, each targeting a specific phase of information linkage: Textual Fingerprinting, Vertical Knowledge Filtering, and Numerical Traceability.

Identity Resolution via Textual Fingerprints (Task 1). In this task, the agent is presented with a semantically generic yet syntactically unique text snippet (e.g., a philosophical reflection on economics from a course note). It must resolve the author’s identity and cross-reference their activity on a specific platform, such as their GitHub contribution frequency on a specific UTC date. To ensure difficulty, we employ Adversarial Lexical Selection for the anchor text, purposefully injecting high-frequency terminology to maximize lexical collision in standard search indices and neutralize simple keyword matching. Furthermore, the task enforces Cross-Domain Hopping between unstructured academic content and structured commit logs. By targeting niche repositories and demanding precise timestamps, we ensure the query bypasses the “direct answer” features of commercial search engines, necessitating deep page parsing.

Hierarchical Filtering in Vertical Knowledge Bases (Task 2). This task requires the agent to identify a target entity (e.g., a fund management company) that satisfies a conjunction of strict quantitative constraints across disjoint temporal windows on a single webpage (e.g., Net Asset Value at T1T_{1} and Total Shares at T2T_{2}). Upon successful identification, the agent executes a secondary query regarding a dynamic attribute, such as new personnel qualifications within a narrow, recent time frame. Unlike open-domain QA, this simulates Vertical Search. The large-scale financial figures constrain the search space but strictly require Schema Awareness—the agent must know where to look (e.g., official regulatory disclosures) rather than just what to look for. Additionally, a Temporal Precision constraint using data from the immediate past prevents the model from relying on memorized parametric knowledge, forcing real-time interaction with dynamic web environments.

Inverse Entity Resolution via Numerical Fingerprinting (Task 3). In this task, the agent receives a set of obscure numerical rankings (e.g., specific performance rankings of four different products) serving as a unique “numerical fingerprint” for a specific fund manager. The objective is to decode the manager’s identity and trace their career trajectory back to a distant historical point, such as their employer ten years prior. This design relies on Anti-Shortcut Engineering. We intentionally sample rankings from the long tail (e.g., 130th or 746th) rather than the head. While top rankings are heavily covered in news articles—providing trivial shortcuts—mid-tier rankings force the agent to query raw performance databases, demanding granular data processing. Moreover, the Temporal Multi-hop aspect tests the agent’s ability to maintain identity persistence across time. It links an instantaneous current state to a static historical attribute, heavily penalizing agents prone to hallucinating based on current affiliations.

4.2 Type II: Consistency via V-Structures (Pullbacks)

While Type I evaluates linear connectivity, Type II evaluates the agent’s capacity to model V-structures, formally known as pullbacks in category theory. In these tasks, the agent must retrieve information from disjoint sources (S1,S2,…,SnS_{1},S_{2},\dots,S_{n}) and synthesize them to discover latent constraints, verify intersections, or detect conflicts.

The core challenge lies in the asymmetry of synthesis: while individual data points are computationally trivial to retrieve, recognizing their necessary intersection requires profound structural awareness. To systematically benchmark this capability, we design five abstract task paradigms, each instantiated through complex, real-world scenarios.

Distributed Quantitative Synthesis (Task 4). This task requires the agent to deduce a specific metric by synthesizing sparse, interdependent quantitative constraints scattered across non-adjacent structural nodes, such as disparate temporal reports. Because the target answer does not exist verbatim on the web, this setup forces implicit equation solving. The agent must retrieve multiple disconnected documents, align their dynamic data schemas, formulate an algebraic relationship using a provided delta (e.g., a growth value), and solve for the unknown. To prevent the model from relying on memorized parametric knowledge or high-level summaries, we enforce anti-memorization via long-tail sampling (e.g., querying the 7th largest holding of a fund), thereby necessitating raw, multi-document data extraction and mathematical alignment.

Entity Resolution under Hard-Negative Interference (Task 5). In this task, the agent must accurately profile a specific entity using a rigid, unique designator while navigating severe probabilistic distractors that share identical superficial features. We employ adversarial attribute injection by constructing scenarios where the target entity—defined strictly by a unique ID—is an obscure figure, whereas the “hard negative” distractor is a high-profile individual sharing the exact same name. This paradigm stress-tests the tension between parametric prior and contextual fact. It evaluates whether the agent anchors its reasoning on the deterministic pullback (faithfully matching the ID to the correct person) or hallucinates by falling back on its pre-training distribution (lazily matching the name to the famous entity).

Implicit Boundary Condition Detection (Task 6). In this task, the agent is presented with a standard operational instruction, but the true objective is for it to autonomously discover and apply an unmentioned, domain-specific boundary condition that mathematically invalidates the instruction. Unlike traditional reasoning benchmarks that explicitly provide the rules, deep research requires meta-cognitive rule triggering—discovering the necessity of a rule in the first place. We instantiate this using a hypothetical financial trade that exceeds a statutory limit. The agent must independently realize that the action is bounded by compliance laws, retrieve real-time baseline data (e.g., net asset value), and compute the intersection to flag the latent violation.

Cross-Domain Anomaly Intersection (Task 7). In this task, the agent receives a seemingly benign user request that covertly embeds partial, fragmented identifiers matching an entity in an external, open-world risk database. This requires a fuzzy database join. Although not explicitly instructed to perform a background check, regulatory compliance implicitly dictates it. We instantiate this by embedding the partial identity features of a fugitive into a routine customer service scenario. This creates a structural conflict between helpfulness (executing the user’s task) and systemic constraints (flagging the anomaly), rigorously testing the agent’s capacity for unprompted anomaly detection across disparate domains—a direct test of safety alignment override.

Latent Dependency Satisfiability (Task 8). In this task, we disguise a dependency conflict problem within a dense, unstructured narrative. The agent must look past domain-specific jargon and narrative flow to perform unstructured constraint extraction, ultimately identifying the underlying structural graph and any logical contradictions. For systemic conflict resolution, we instantiate this paradigm by describing a multi-year software setup timeline. By anchoring specific library installations to historical timestamps, the agent must synthesize the temporal context, retrieve historical compatibility matrices, and identify latent mutual exclusivity—such as version conflicts that render the described outcome physically impossible.

4.3 Type III: Organization via Substructure Re-ordering

While Type I and Type II evaluate the discovery of existing connections and intersections, Type III tests the agent’s capacity to act as an structure processor—specifically, its ability to perform substructure re-ordering. In categorical terms, this is analogous to applying a sorting functor to construct a strictly ordered subcategory from chaotic data, and subsequently evaluating limits or tracing morphisms exclusively within that newly formed topological structure.

Because commercial search engines inherently return flat, relevance-based results, Type III tasks force the agent to override this default topology. The agent must impose a strict mathematical ordering (e.g., ranking by floating-point values) on retrieved raw data, using this dynamically generated ordered list as an anchor for complex downstream reasoning. We formalize this capability through four distinct task paradigms.

Rank-Conditioned Temporal Multi-Hop (Task 9). In this task, the agent must identify an entity based on a dynamic ordinal rank (e.g., the 5th highest-performing asset) at a specific discrete time T1T_{1}. Once resolved, the agent executes a temporal jump to retrieve a highly volatile, state-dependent attribute of that entity at a distant historical time T2T_{2}. This design deliberately breaks search index shortcuts. Because search engines index static names rather than daily dynamic ranks, the agent must autonomously construct the Top-NN substructure, extract the kk-th element, and only then formulate the secondary query. Furthermore, to enforce temporal state precision, T2T_{2} is strategically chosen to be a date immediately following a state transition (e.g., right after a manager resigns). This severely penalizes agents that hallucinate based on parametric priors or historical averages.

Range-Bounded Topological Sorting (Task 10). In this task, the agent is required to filter a massive, cross-sectional dataset using a continuous floating-point interval [a,b][a,b], dynamically generating a strict ordinal ranking of the resulting substructure from highest to lowest. This paradigm demands algorithmic exhaustiveness. Commercial search engines cannot natively execute granular queries like “return all entities with a growth rate between 7.3% and 7.6%.” Consequently, the agent must autonomously retrieve broad macro-level data tables, internalize the context, and act as a deterministic filtering and sorting algorithm. This serves as a rigorous stress test for the LLM’s inherent numerical reasoning and its ability to perform granular float-point comparison without omitting entities near the boundary conditions.

Top-KK Substructure Aggregation and Synthesis (Task 11). In this task, after retrieving and establishing a strictly ordered Top-KK substructure based on a primary metric XX (e.g., daily growth rate), the agent must compute macroscopic statistical invariants—such as the mean, variance, or mathematical range—over a parallel metric YY (e.g., net asset value) across those KK entities. This requires Map-Reduce cognitive emulation, evaluating whether a dynamically re-ordered substructure can serve as a stable foundation for complex mathematical synthesis. It heavily probes context window integrity. Calculating an aggregate statistic forces an operation over the entire constructed subcategory, aggressively penalizing any data omission or alignment hallucination while the agent holds multiple distinct entities in its working memory.

Rank-Anchored Time-Series Computation (Task 12). In this task, the agent identifies a target entity via its ordinal rank on a singular discrete timestamp TrankT_{\text{rank}}. It must then pivot its analytical lens to a continuous temporal window [Tstart,Tend][T_{\text{start}},T_{\text{end}}] to compute a longitudinal time-series statistic (e.g., the volatility or range of cumulative values) for that specific entity. This necessitates orthogonal dimension shifting. The agent must seamlessly switch between two fundamentally different retrieval modalities: cross-sectional retrieval (evaluating all entities on a single day to establish the rank) and longitudinal retrieval (evaluating a single entity across multiple days). Ultimately, this demands complex working memory, ensuring the agent maintains rigorous schema isolation and does not conflate the metric used for initial ranking with the metric required for the downstream time-series computation.

4.4 Type IV: Structure Validity via the Yoneda Probe

The ultimate hallmark of an autonomous Deep Research Agent lies not merely in its ability to retrieve existing information, but in its capacity to confidently prove non-existence. Rooted in the philosophy of falsification and the Yoneda Lemma (Mac Lane, 2013), Type IV tasks evaluate the agent’s ability to authenticate the ontological reality of an entity (or attribute) by exhaustively probing its external mappings (morphisms) within the knowledge space 𝒲\mathcal{W}. If an entity does not interact with the real world—yielding null retrieval morphisms—the agent must halt execution and refute the premise, rather than fabricating a hallucinated structure.

Large language models inherently suffer from severe sycophancy and premise acceptance. If a user’s prompt implies the existence of a document or a data field, the agent’s parametric prior strongly biases it to fulfill the instruction via hallucination. To benchmark the agent’s zero-shot resistance to these presuppositional traps, we design three adversarial task paradigms.

Schema-Level Asymmetry and Null-Field Refutation (Task 13). In this task the agent is tasked with extracting a highly specific, quantitative metric (e.g., the asset scale of the largest underlying holding) across a batch of peer entities, such as the Q1 investment reports for five distinct fund companies. Crucially, while the reports exist for all entities, the target data field is structurally omitted by a subset of them. This paradigm deliberately induces peer-pressure hallucination to test for local non-existence. By batching valid entities with missing data alongside entities that do contain the data, we create structural peer pressure. The agent is heavily biased to maintain output symmetry (e.g., generating a complete, densely populated table) and will often hallucinate the missing metrics based on surrounding context. To succeed, the agent must perform an exhaustive null-verification of the specific reports, explicitly recognize the absence of the schema field, and correctly report the ∅\emptyset state, proving that its output is strictly bounded by retrieved evidence rather than structural expectation.

Macro-Ontological Invalidity via the Phantom Entity Probe (Task 14). In this task, the agent is instructed to interpret the “core arguments” of a completely fabricated, non-existent report attributed to a high-authority source, covering an absurd interdisciplinary topic (e.g., a Goldman Sachs report on “Quantum Encryption in Modern Agricultural Irrigation”). Testing for global non-existence, the difficulty here lies in the adversarial combination of a high-trust anchor and syntactically plausible academic jargon, pitting authority bias against ground truth. The agent must execute a Yoneda Falsification. Upon conducting a broad exploratory search and finding zero legitimate incoming or outgoing references (Hom​(X,Y)=∅\text{Hom}(X,Y)=\emptyset) to this exact report, it must use this absolute absence of connectivity to formally deduce the non-existence of the object itself, refusing to generate plausible arguments from its parametric memory.

Asymmetric Comparative Hallucination (Task 15). In this task, the prompt demands a granular comparative analysis between two highly correlated entities (e.g., the 2024 annual reports of CATL and EVE Energy) regarding a highly plausible latent feature, such as specific wording in the “Geopolitical Risk in the Middle East” section. However, this specific feature exists in at most one of the reports. LLMs are highly optimized to follow comparative instructions; therefore, when object AA possesses feature ff but object BB lacks it, the instruction creates a massive probabilistic gradient for the model to hallucinate f⁡(B)f(B) in order to execute the comparison—a phenomenon we term instruction-forced feature alignment. To pass this stress test, the agent must actively engage in breaking the relational presupposition. It must realize that the prerequisite for comparison is invalid, break the requested instruction format, and declare an asymmetric falsification, thereby proving its allegiance to factual topology over user-defined operational flow.

5 Experiments

To rigorously assess the capability boundaries of current state-of-the-art systems and ensure a comprehensive, equitable comparison, we evaluate the performance of 1111 leading mainstream models and AI products. To capture diverse problem-solving paradigms, these models are carefully selected to span three core competencies: complex reasoning, information retrieval (search), and autonomous deep research. Accordingly, we categorize them into the following three groups:

  • •

    Reasoning Models (5 products): Gemini-3-pro-Reasoning (API) Google (2026), Claude-4.5-Sonnet-Reasoning Anthropic (2025), Doubao-Reasoning (API) ByteDance (2025), GPT-5-Reasoning (API) OpenAI (2025), Qwen3-Reasoning (API) Qwen Team (2025).

  • •

    Search-augmented Models (3 products): Qwen3-Search (web) Team (2026), Doubao-Search (web) ByteDance (2025), Perplexity-Sonar-Pro-Search Perplexity (2025).

  • •

    Deep Research Agents (3 products): Doubao Deep Research (web), Qwen Deep Research (web), Grok Deep Research (web) xAI (2025).

For task evaluation, we adopt a strict binary scoring metric (00 for failure, 11 for success) to establish clear and unambiguous performance boundaries. To mitigate the inherent biases and potential hallucinations of automated evaluators while maintaining evaluation scalability, we implement a robust hybrid evaluation pipeline that integrates the “LLM-as-a-Judge” paradigm with meticulous human verification. Specifically, we first deploy GPT-5 to generate initial automated assessments based on predefined rubrics. Subsequently, domain experts conduct a comprehensive manual review of these preliminary scores. This rigorous two-stage verification process guarantees the utmost reliability, objectivity, and correctness of our final benchmark results.

5.1 Evaluation Results

Table 2 summarizes the evaluation results across the four task paradigms, with the average score of each type calculated among all samples. While the overall performance remains universally low, Grok Deep Research raises the best-performing total average to 19.9%. Crucially, the results reveal a massive capability variance within the Deep Research models. Despite this state-of-the-art established by Grok, the near-floor baseline of other deep research implementations highlights the severe difficulty of the benchmark and exposes critical limitations in how autonomous loops are currently optimized. A more detailed per-task score can be found in Appendix C.

Current models still struggle significantly with structural synthesis and multi-step verification. Tasks requiring the traversal of obscure linkages (Type I) or the resolution of V-structure pullbacks (Type II) proved highly challenging. This exposes the practical impact of retrieval-verification asymmetry. While Grok Deep Research pushes the boundary in resolving V-structures to achieve a leading 4.9% in Type II, its low Type I score (1.5%) and the near-zero success rates of other models indicate that multi-hop structural reasoning remains a formidable bottleneck even for advanced autonomous loops.

Advanced Deep Research pipelines redefine topological re-ordering capabilities. When tasked with disentangling complex dependencies and imposing mathematical ordering on flat search results (Type III), pure reasoning models largely fail. Previously, search-augmented models like Doubao w/Search (16.3%) demonstrated a clear advantage. However, Grok Deep Research now dominates this type with 26.3%. This suggests that while intrinsic parametric reasoning alone cannot override default search topologies, a highly optimized deep research agent can more effectively integrate retrieval mechanisms with structural heuristics compared to simpler search-augmentation paradigms.

Top-tier autonomous agents can successfully resist the sycophancy trap. The Yoneda Probe tasks (Type IV), designed to evaluate ontological verification and resistance to hallucinated premises, yield a profound insight into implementation variance. While most deep research agents (e.g., Qwen Deep Research at 4.1%) perform poorly—trapped in recursive attempts to satisfy the prompt’s false premise—this is not an inescapable flaw of the paradigm. Grok Deep Research successfully matches the rigorous falsification priors of the best pure reasoning models (Qwen3 w/Reasoning), with both achieving a benchmark-leading 46.9%. This proves that advanced agentic loops can yield null retrieval morphisms without succumbing to hallucination.

State-of-the-art Deep Research highlights a profound implementation gap. The extreme variance in task-specific performance previously highlighted a fragmented landscape across different paradigms. However, the most striking fragmentation now exists within the Deep Research agents itself. While most deep research agents fail to synergize their components effectively, Grok Deep Research shatters this trend by securing the highest scores across Type II, Type III, Type IV, and the Total Average. This stark internal disparity empirically validates that while building a robust autonomous agent is notoriously difficult, top-tier implementations demonstrate the capacity to organically unify topological manipulation with rigorous falsification priors.

Universal collapse on specific configurations. A granular inspection reveals the existence of absolute structural blind spots. Specifically, Task 10 (within Type III) and Task 13 (within Type IV) continue to yield a general 0.0% success rate across all evaluated models. While Grok Deep Research manages to break the deadlock on Task 12 (achieving 10.0%), the enduring failure of all systems on Tasks 10 and 13 indicates that certain specific mathematical constraints and extreme presuppositional traps completely neutralize current AI paradigms. These hard failures suggest that merely scaling current methods may be insufficient to resolve these fundamental structural deficits.

Extreme intra-type variance reveals a lingering reliance on brittle heuristics. While models occasionally succeed within a broader task paradigm, their performance at the individual task level remains highly localized and zero-inflated. This phenomenon persists even within state-of-the-art architectures. For instance, in resolving V-structure pullbacks (Type II), while earlier models showed isolated spikes (e.g., GPT-5 w/Reasoning and Qwen3 w/Search achieving 20.0% on Task 7), Grok Deep Research similarly exhibits fragmentation, scoring 8.3% on Task 5 and 4.0% on Task 7, but completely failing Tasks 4, 6, and 8. Likewise, in Type III, Grok matches the previous peak of 25.0% on Task 11 and breaks through on Task 12, yet still fails Task 10 entirely. This drastic intra-type variance suggests that despite macro-level improvements, localized successes may still be influenced by task-specific artifacts or fortuitous latent associations, indicating that a systemic, generalized mastery of structural mapping and intersection verification has yet to be achieved.

5.2 Disentangling the SS and RR Scores

Existing deep research agent benchmarks usually rely on monolithic, binary accuracy metrics. When an agent fails a complex open-ended query, a simple “zero” score offers little diagnostic visibility into the underlying cause.

To make the evaluation process more fine-grained, we introduce a dual-weighting diagnostic system for each task, denoted as the Search Score (SS) and the Reasoning Score (RR). A detailed rubrics shown in Table 4 in the Appendix B, these weights represent a deliberate, analytical allocation of the task’s primary performance bottleneck, summing to 100%100\%. Crucially, they directly map to the theoretical difficulty of successfully executing the Search Functor and the Reasoning Functor.

Source and Derivation of the Scores. The SS and RR scores are not arbitrarily assigned; they are intrinsically derived from the design of each task paradigm. The SS-score quantifies the adversarial complexity of the retrieval path. Conversely, the RR-score quantifies the cognitive load required to process the retrieved context. By explicitly decoupling these two dimensions, our tasks span a comprehensive diagnostic spectrum. The purpose of introducing the SS and RR scores is to shift the paradigm of agent evaluation from outcome-based scoring to more process-based diagnosis. For researchers and developers, this provides an actionable compass.

To move beyond monolithic accuracy metrics, Table 3 presents a detailed diagnosis by decoupling model performance into explicit Search (SS) and Reasoning (RR) scores. The results clearly validate this diagnostic framework by revealing distinct capability bottlenecks and a stark performance variance, particularly within the Deep Research paradigm. While specialized models demonstrate isolated strengths—with Qwen3 w/Reasoning leading cognitive management (RR-score 12.8) and Doubao w/Search leading retrieval navigation (SS-score 4.4)—Deep Research models exhibit highly heterogeneous results. Some deep research models exhibit suppressed scores across both dimensions, failing to organically synthesize the Search and Reasoning Functors in autonomous loops. However, Grok Deep Research drastically breaks this mold, achieving an unprecedented SS-score of 11.8 and an RR-score of 21.6. This fine-grained breakdown empirically confirms that while the deep research pipeline may prone to compromised retrieval trajectories and diminished reasoning capacity, top-tier implementations can overcome these architectural bottlenecks and truly make the agent loop helpful.

6 Related Works

Category Theory in AI.

Category theory has provided profound mathematical foundations for various branches of artificial intelligence (Shiebler et al., 2021), spanning backpropagation (Fong et al., 2019), probability (Fritz, 2020), conditional independence (Mahadevan, 2022a), and core learning paradigms (Harris, 2019; Mahadevan, 2022b). Recent advancements have successfully applied a categorical lens to natural language (Bradley et al., 2022), foundation models (Yuan, 2023), and the functional equivalence of neural representations (Chen et al., 2023). Although prior works construct categories and functors specific to those respective areas, our work proposes a novel formalization: establishing a categorical framework to explicitly model the ideal behavior of deep research agents.

Deep Research Benchmarks.

Traditional QA and reasoning datasets, including prominent suites like GAIA (Mialon et al., 2023), WebWalker (Wu et al., 2025), and WebShaper (Tao et al., 2025), have successfully measured analytical capabilities but typically bypass the research phase by providing pre-packaged context. Attempts to introduce open-domain data gathering often fall short by relying on static historical archives Bigeard et al., 2025. This static nature inadvertently tests a model’s internal memory rather than its active, exploratory search proficiency Wei et al. (2025).

To properly assess deep research agents, the evaluation paradigm must shift from static data processing to dynamic, end-to-end autonomy. Pioneering works in this direction evaluate interactive tool use: DeepResearchBench (Du et al., 2025) introduces metrics to evaluate open-ended report generation. The BrowseComp series (Wei et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025) sets standards for persistent web navigation and creative search tactics, while FinSearchComp (Hu et al., 2025) designs time-sensitive tasks for financial contexts. However, there remains an urgent need for a theoretically-grounded evaluation paradigm designed specifically for complex, goal-directed QA tasks that can systematically evaluate the concrete capabilities of deep research agents.

7 Conclusion

We address the absence of theoretically grounded evaluations for Deep Research Agents (DRAs) by introducing a category-theoretic benchmark. Conceptualizing the research pipeline as a structural mapping, we transition from fragmented heuristics to systematic stress-testing along four precise axes: simple chains, V-structures, substructure re-ordering, and the Yoneda Probe.

Our human-verified evaluation of 1111 leading models exposes the profound difficulty of formal structural stress-testing. The persistently low baseline, peaking at a 19.9%19.9\% average, empirically validates this extreme challenge. While models universally struggle to traverse sequential connections and verify multi-source intersections, highly optimized DRAs have successfully redefined topological re-ordering. Furthermore, Yoneda Probes reveal that top-tier DRAs can resist the “sycophancy trap”—refuting that active retrieval loops inevitably exacerbate hallucination—and match the rigorous falsification priors of pure reasoning models.

However, massive internal capability variance and absolute structural blind spots demonstrate that merely wrapping reasoning LLMs in ad-hoc search loops remains brittle. While state-of-the-art implementations can organically unify search and reasoning, their enduring reliance on task-specific heuristics highlights that generalized structural mastery remains unsolved. We hope our framework catalyzes a fundamental shift toward a systemic understanding of complex topologies in future deep research architectures.

Appendix A Detailed Proofs

Theorem A.1 (Categorical Validity of Agentic State Spaces).

Let 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, 𝒲\mathcal{W}, 𝐒𝐮𝐛⁡(𝒲)\mathbf{Sub}(\mathcal{W}), and 𝒜\mathcal{A} be the agentic state spaces equipped with their respective objects and relations. If we define the morphisms in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, 𝒲\mathcal{W}, and 𝒜\mathcal{A} as above, then all four spaces strictly satisfy the Eilenberg-Mac Lane axioms and thus constitute mathematically valid categories.

Proof.

To rigorously prove that a given structure forms a category, we must verify the existence of identity morphisms for all objects, the closure under morphism composition, and the associativity of said composition.

1. The Intent Category 𝒬\mathcal{Q} (Query Space):

We model 𝒬\mathcal{Q} as a thin category (a preorder) where at most one morphism exists between any two queries.

  • •

    Identity: For any query q∈Ob⁡(𝒬)q\in\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{Q}), resolving qq trivially depends on itself. Thus, we assign the identity morphism idq:q→q\mathrm{id}_{q}:q\to q.

  • •

    Composition: Let q1,q2,q3∈Ob⁡(𝒬)q_{1},q_{2},q_{3}\in\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{Q}). If f:q1→depq2f:q_{1}\xrightarrow{\text{dep}}q_{2} (resolving q2q_{2} depends on q1q_{1}) and g:q2→depq3g:q_{2}\xrightarrow{\text{dep}}q_{3} (resolving q3q_{3} depends on q2q_{2}), then by the transitive nature of task execution, resolving q3q_{3} inherently necessitates resolving q1q_{1}. Thus, the composite morphism g∘f:q1→depq3g\circ f:q_{1}\xrightarrow{\text{dep}}q_{3} universally exists in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

  • •

    Associativity: Since 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is a preorder defined by logical dependency, any sequence of dependencies trivially satisfies h∘(g∘f)=(h∘g)∘fh\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f.

2. The Knowledge Category 𝒲\mathcal{W} (Web Space):

To ensure compositional closure, we define the morphisms of 𝒲\mathcal{W} as the paths (the free category construction) generated by the directed graph of hyperlinks and direct causal premises.

  • •

    Identity: For any web entity w∈Ob⁡(𝒲)w\in\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{W}), it trivially serves as a premise for its own semantic content. This constitutes the empty path, serving as the identity morphism idw:w→w\mathrm{id}_{w}:w\to w.

  • •

    Composition: If there exists an evidentiary path f:w1→refw2f:w_{1}\xrightarrow{\text{ref}}w_{2} and another path g:w2→refw3g:w_{2}\xrightarrow{\text{ref}}w_{3}, the concatenation of these paths forms a valid, continuous evidentiary chain from w1w_{1} to w3w_{3}. This concatenation forms the composite morphism g∘f∈Hom𝒲​(w1,w3)g\circ f\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{W}}(w_{1},w_{3}).

  • •

    Associativity: Path concatenation is strictly associative; concatenating paths ff, gg, and hh in sequence yields the exact same evidentiary chain regardless of grouping, strictly satisfying h∘(g∘f)=(h∘g)∘fh\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f.

3. The Retrieval Subcategory 𝐒𝐮𝐛⁡(𝒲)\mathbf{Sub}(\mathcal{W}):

  • •

    Identity: For any retrieved subgraph G∈Ob⁡(𝐒𝐮𝐛⁡(𝒲))G\in\mathrm{Ob}(\mathbf{Sub}(\mathcal{W})), the subset relation is reflexive (G⊆GG\subseteq G). This defines the identity inclusion map idG:G↪G\mathrm{id}_{G}:G\hookrightarrow G.

  • •

    Composition: Let G1,G2,G3G_{1},G_{2},G_{3} be subgraphs. If i:G1↪G2i:G_{1}\hookrightarrow G_{2} and j:G2↪G3j:G_{2}\hookrightarrow G_{3} are inclusion mappings, standard set theory guarantees G1⊆G3G_{1}\subseteq G_{3}. The function composition of two inclusions is inherently an inclusion mapping j∘i:G1↪G3j\circ i:G_{1}\hookrightarrow G_{3}, ensuring closure.

  • •

    Associativity: Because morphisms here are literal functions (inclusion maps) acting on sets, their composition inherits the strict associativity of standard function composition.

4. The Reasoning Category 𝒜\mathcal{A} (Logic Space):

We model 𝒜\mathcal{A} analogously to a deductive system (a propositional category).

  • •

    Identity: For any proposition a∈Ob⁡(𝒜)a\in\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{A}), the implication a⟹aa\implies a is a fundamental logical tautology (the law of identity). This serves as the identity morphism ida:a→a\mathrm{id}_{a}:a\to a.

  • •

    Composition: If we have logical entailments f:a1⟹a2f:a_{1}\implies a_{2} and g:a2⟹a3g:a_{2}\implies a_{3}, the rule of hypothetical syllogism dictates that a1a_{1} must logically entail a3a_{3}. The proof of this chained entailment serves as the composite morphism g∘f:a1⟹a3g\circ f:a_{1}\implies a_{3}.

  • •

    Associativity: In formal deductive logic, the sequential application of modus ponens or hypothetical syllogism over a chain of propositions is invariant to the order of proof construction, yielding h∘(g∘f)=(h∘g)∘fh\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f.

Since all four spaces strictly satisfy the requirements for objects, hom-sets, identities, composition, and associativity, they are categorically valid. ∎

Proposition A.2 (Chain-of-Search Consistency).

An ideal deep research agent preserves compositionality during multi-hop retrieval (deep search). For a sequence of sub-task dependencies q1→𝑓q2→𝑔q3q_{1}\xrightarrow{f}q_{2}\xrightarrow{g}q_{3}, it strictly holds that S⁡(g∘f)=S⁡(g)∘S⁡(f)S(g\circ f)=S(g)\circ S(f).

Proof.

This proposition captures the core contradiction of deep research: the tension between end-to-end execution and step-by-step decomposition. The left-hand side, S⁡(g∘f)S(g\circ f), represents the evidence chain obtained by directly executing a multi-hop query. The right-hand side, S⁡(g)∘S⁡(f)S(g)\circ S(f), represents the evidence pieced together by explicitly decomposing the compound problem into sub-problems.

An ideal agent requires these two approaches to yield consistent evidence graphs. However, a prominent failure case in LLMs is Material Loss during long-chain search. When processing an extended research trajectory S⁡(g∘f)S(g\circ f), the agent often breaks the chain by dropping intermediate nodes, whereas the step-by-step approach S⁡(g)∘S⁡(f)S(g)\circ S(f) remains complete. If intermediate routing evidence is lost, the equality is broken, demonstrating that long-horizon context truncation is mathematically equivalent to the violation of search compositionality. ∎

Proposition A.3 (Functoriality and Transitivity of Deduction).

By the composition axiom of functors, an ideal reasoning agent inherently preserves deductive transitivity. For any composable evidentiary morphisms w1→𝑓w2→𝑔w3w_{1}\xrightarrow{f}w_{2}\xrightarrow{g}w_{3} in 𝒲\mathcal{W}, it strictly holds that R⁡(g∘f)=R⁡(g)∘R⁡(f)R(g\circ f)=R(g)\circ R(f).

Proof.

The forward claim is a direct consequence of the functoriality axiom: a valid functor must rigorously preserve morphism composition. By definition of a category, the evidentiary composite g∘f∈Hom𝒲​(w1,w3)g\circ f\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{W}}(w_{1},w_{3}) universally exists.

Evaluating the converse direction serves as a precise diagnostic for reasoning failure. Suppose the agent successfully deduces the local, step-by-step implications R⁡(f)R(f) and R⁡(g)R(g), but synthesizes an end-to-end assertion hagent∈Hom𝒜​(R⁡(w1),R⁡(w3))h_{\mathrm{agent}}\in\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(R(w_{1}),R(w_{3})) spanning the full context. If hagent≠R⁡(g)∘R⁡(f)h_{\mathrm{agent}}\neq R(g)\circ R(f), a specific categorical breakdown has occurred: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Degradation. Because the composite g∘fg\circ f exists and dictates the correct transitive logic R⁡(g∘f)R(g\circ f), asserting an inequality proves that the agent failed to faithfully propagate the intermediate causal constraints (w2w_{2}) into its composed deduction. The inequality exactly identifies the locus where the agent’s long-context logical synthesis becomes mathematically unsound. ∎
